\chapter{Standing Alone}
\label{ch:fr-pronouns}
\hlchaptermodality{43}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask who and what, and use the pronouns that stand on their own instead of leaning on a verb.}

Every person and every thing the book owns is asked about and answered. One accident runs under three of the chapter's four pairs: a pronoun that lived unstressed in front of a verb wore down, and the one that stood alone kept its weight -- which is why French has que and quoi, je and moi, tu and toi, and only one elle.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[qui]{qui — \textquotedblleft{}who,\textquotedblright{} the word Latin barely changed}

\label{lesson:FR-C39-qui}



\begin{quote}
Five question words are yours — \emph{où, quand, comment, combien, pourquoi}. Every one of them asks about a circumstance. None of them can ask about a \textbf{person}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the pronoun that was Latin for \emph{man} — \emph{on}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{qui} — who.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Qui est-ce ?} — Who is it? · \textbf{Qui est là ?} — Who's there?
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{quis}, and almost nothing has happened to it. That is unusual: most French words are half the length of their Latin parents — \emph{aqua} to \emph{eau}, \emph{calidus} to \emph{chaud} — and this one lost a single consonant in two thousand years.

The \textbf{qu-} is the same opening that starts \emph{quand}, \emph{quel} and \emph{combien}'s cousins, and English carries it in the borrowed words \textbf{query}, \textbf{question} and \textbf{quest}.

One thing to watch: \textbf{qui} never elides. \emph{Qui est} stays two clean words where \emph{que} would have become \emph{qu'}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{qui} — one syllable, \emph{kee}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Qui est-ce ?\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Qui est là ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask, then answer with what you own — \textquotedblleft{}Qui est-ce ? — C'est ma mère.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Qui est ici ? — Voici mon ami.\textquotedblright{}
  \item asked about several people, with the plural you cannot hear — \textquotedblleft{}Qui sont les amis ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the six question words together — \textquotedblleft{}qui, où, quand, comment, combien, pourquoi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{qui}? (\emph{\textbf{Quis}}, one letter shorter.) Does it elide before a vowel? (\textbf{No} — \emph{qui est}, two clean words.) Ask who somebody is and answer with your mother.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[que]{que — \textquotedblleft{}what,\textquotedblright{} and the word that always elides}

\label{lesson:FR-C39-que}



\begin{quote}
You have said \textbf{que} twice already without meeting it: inside \textbf{est-ce que} and inside \textbf{parce que}. Say both.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{que} — what.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Qu'est-ce que c'est ?} — What is it?
\end{quote}

\textbf{qui} and \textbf{que} are Latin \textbf{quis} and \textbf{quid} — the \emph{who} and the \emph{what} of one pronoun, kept as a pair. French has both halves where English rebuilt its own from a different root.

Unlike \emph{qui}, \textbf{que} always elides before a vowel, and that is why the commonest question in French looks so alarming on the page. \textbf{Qu'est-ce que c'est} is four ordinary words: \emph{que} + \emph{est-ce} + \emph{que} + \emph{c'est} — \textquotedblleft{}what is it that this is.\textquotedblright{} Said aloud it is three syllables, \emph{kess-kuh-SAY}, and it is the first thing a learner should be able to say without thinking.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the big one, slowly, then fast — \textquotedblleft{}Qu'est-ce que c'est ?\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{kess-kuh-SAY}
  \item the four pieces — \emph{que, est-ce, que, c'est}
  \item ask and answer — \textquotedblleft{}Qu'est-ce que c'est ? — C'est du pain.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Qui est-ce ?\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}Qu'est-ce que c'est ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask about an action — \textquotedblleft{}Qu'est-ce que tu finis ?\textquotedblright{} and the plural that grows a syllable, \textquotedblleft{}Qu'est-ce que vous finissez ?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the pair elides? (\emph{\textbf{Que}}.) What four words are inside \emph{qu'est-ce que c'est}? (\emph{\textbf{Que, est-ce, que, c'est}}.) Which asks about a person and which about a thing?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quoi]{quoi — \textquotedblleft{}what,\textquotedblright{} standing on its own two feet}

\label{lesson:FR-C39-quoi}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{que}. Now try to say it alone, as a one-word question. It cannot be done — the word is too light to stand up.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{quoi} — what, when it has to carry weight.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Quoi ?} — What? · \textbf{De quoi ?} — Of what? · \textbf{À quoi ?} — To what?
\end{quote}

\textbf{que} and \textbf{quoi} are the same Latin \textbf{quid}, twice. One of them spent centuries unstressed in front of a verb and wore down to a single silent-\emph{e} syllable; the other spent those centuries alone or after a preposition, where it had to be heard, and kept its weight.

So the split is not a rule somebody invented. It is one word that lived two different lives in two different positions.

The practical test is short: \textbf{que} leans on something and \textbf{quoi} does not. After a preposition — \emph{de}, \emph{à} — only \emph{quoi} will do.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item alone — \textquotedblleft{}Quoi ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item after a preposition — \textquotedblleft{}De quoi ?\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}À quoi ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Qu'est-ce que c'est ?\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}C'est quoi ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item all three pronouns — \textquotedblleft{}qui, que, quoi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two can stand alone? (\emph{\textbf{Quoi}}.) Which one follows a preposition? (\emph{\textbf{Quoi}}.) What single Latin word are both? (\emph{\textbf{Quid}} — worn two ways by two positions.) Say all three pronouns.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[moi et toi]{moi et toi — the pronouns that can stand alone}

\label{lesson:FR-C39-moi-toi}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Je} and \textbf{tu} cannot stand alone either — they must lean on a verb. You have seen that happen to \emph{que} in the last lesson, and the same accident produced the same result here.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{moi} — me. · \textbf{toi} — you, informally.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Moi ?} — Me? · \textbf{Et toi ?} — And you? · \textbf{C'est moi.} — It's me.
\end{quote}

You have said \textbf{et toi ?} and \textbf{et vous ?} for a long time as a fixed piece of conversation. This is the word inside it.

\textbf{je} and \textbf{moi} are one Latin pronoun, \textbf{tu} and \textbf{toi} are another, and each split for the reason \emph{que} and \emph{quoi} split: the form that lived unstressed in front of a verb wore down, and the form that stood alone or after a preposition kept its weight. Three pairs, one accident.

The polite twin of \emph{toi} is \textbf{vous}, which does both jobs and does not split — \emph{et vous ?} is the same word as the \emph{vous} in \emph{vous parlez}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item alone — \textquotedblleft{}Moi ?\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Toi ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the phrase you already had — \textquotedblleft{}Ça va bien, et toi ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item politely — \textquotedblleft{}Et vous ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}C'est moi.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}C'est toi.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three pairs the same accident made — \textquotedblleft{}je/moi, tu/toi, que/quoi\textquotedblright{}
  \item in the order a sentence holds to, doer first — \textquotedblleft{}Moi, je parle français.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form of \emph{je} stands alone? (\emph{\textbf{Moi}}.) And of \emph{tu}? (\emph{\textbf{Toi}}.) Which earlier pair split the same way? (\emph{\textbf{Que}} and \emph{\textbf{quoi}}.) What is the polite word that does not split? (\emph{\textbf{Vous}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lui et elle]{lui et elle — the third pair, and the one that did not split}

\label{lesson:FR-C39-lui-elle}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Je} became \emph{moi}, \emph{tu} became \emph{toi}. Predict what \emph{il} becomes, then predict what \emph{elle} becomes.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{lui} — him, standing alone. · \textbf{elle} — her, and also \emph{she}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{C'est lui.} — It's him. · \textbf{C'est elle.} — It's her.
\end{quote}

Only half the prediction comes true. \textbf{il} does split, into \textbf{lui} — and \textbf{elle} does not split at all. The same four letters do both jobs: \emph{elle parle} and \emph{c'est elle}.

Nothing decided that except which syllables happened to carry stress in Latin. \emph{Illi} gave \emph{lui}, \emph{ille} gave \emph{il}, and \emph{illa} gave one \emph{elle} that was heavy enough already. The masculine split and the feminine did not, and the language has lived with the asymmetry ever since.

That same \emph{ille} family is where \textbf{le}, \textbf{la} and \textbf{les} came from, so the article and the pronoun in front of you are cousins several times over.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}C'est lui.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}C'est elle.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four that stand alone — \textquotedblleft{}moi, toi, lui, elle\textquotedblright{}
  \item the feminine doing both jobs — \textquotedblleft{}elle parle\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}c'est elle\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask and answer — \textquotedblleft{}Qui est-ce ? — C'est lui.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousins — \textquotedblleft{}il, elle, le, la\textquotedblright{}, all from one Latin family
  \item offer a choice between them — \textquotedblleft{}C'est lui ou c'est elle ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the plural that takes an \emph{x} — \textquotedblleft{}les cheveux de lui\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}les bateaux\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{il} become when it stands alone? (\emph{\textbf{Lui}}.) And \emph{elle}? (\emph{\textbf{Elle}} — it does not change.) Which Latin family gave \emph{il}, \emph{elle}, \emph{le} and \emph{la}? (\emph{\textbf{Ille, illa, illi}} — one family.) Say the four standing pronouns.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Qui est-ce ? — the chapter, run cold}

\label{lesson:FR-R39-qui-est-ce}



\begin{quote}
One accident made three of this chapter's pairs. Name the accident, then name the three pairs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: asking about people and things}
Every person and every thing the book owns, asked about and answered.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item about people — \textquotedblleft{}Qui est-ce ? — C'est ma mère. C'est mon père. C'est mon frère. C'est ma sœur.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Qui est-ce ? — C'est mon ami. C'est l'enfant.\textquotedblright{}
  \item about things — \textquotedblleft{}Qu'est-ce que c'est ? — C'est du pain. C'est du café. C'est du fromage.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the short spoken version — \textquotedblleft{}C'est quoi ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three ways to ask, all still yours — voice, \emph{est-ce que}, inversion
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — standing alone}
The leaning pronouns and the standing ones, side by side.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item leaning — \textquotedblleft{}je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont\textquotedblright{}
  \item standing — \textquotedblleft{}moi, toi, lui, elle\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pairs — \textquotedblleft{}je/moi, tu/toi, il/lui\textquotedblright{} — and the one that did not split, \textquotedblleft{}elle\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same accident on a question word — \textquotedblleft{}que/quoi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the phrase you have had all along — \textquotedblleft{}Ça va bien, et toi ?\textquotedblright{} and politely, \textquotedblleft{}Et vous ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pronoun that took over from \emph{nous} — \textquotedblleft{}On y va.\textquotedblright{}
  \item contrasted — \textquotedblleft{}Moi, oui, mais toi, non.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which question pronoun never elides? (\emph{\textbf{Qui}}.) Which one always does? (\emph{\textbf{Que}}.) Which one stands alone and follows a preposition? (\emph{\textbf{Quoi}}.) And which of the four standing pronouns is the same word as its leaning twin? (\emph{\textbf{Elle}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
